title: Mishpatim: the heart of a stranger (Exodus 23:9)
hook: "for ye know the heart of a stranger, seeing ye were strangers"

segments.voice: Yesterday Mishpatim brought Sinai down into pits, oxen and loans. Your line was holiness lives in details. Which small thing did you do properly? Today, one law in the portion that keeps coming back. Day three hundred forty-nine.

Remember the first day at a new school. Or the first week in a new city, or a new country. You don't know where the bathroom is. You don't know which jokes are allowed. You stand at the edge of a group, holding your tray, trying to look like you're not looking for a seat. Almost everyone has had that feeling at least once. Most of us forget it as soon as we belong. The Torah, in the middle of a list of laws about courts and bribes and fair judgment, asks the Israelites not to forget it.
screen: `THE FIRST DAY, HOLDING YOUR TRAY.` → `LOOKING FOR A SEAT.` → `DON'T FORGET IT.`

segments.voice: Here's the verse, in the old Jewish translation: "And a stranger shalt thou not oppress; for ye know the heart of a stranger, seeing ye were strangers in the land of Egypt." The Hebrew word for stranger is ger. It comes from a root meaning to sojourn, to live somewhere that isn't originally yours. Abraham calls himself a ger when he buys a grave for Sarah: a stranger and a sojourner among the locals. Later, in rabbinic Hebrew, ger also came to mean a convert to Judaism, someone who chose to join the people. But here, in Exodus, it means the outsider living among you: the immigrant, the foreigner, the one without family or land to protect them. And look at the reason given. Not because it's the law. Not because God says so, though God does. Because you know. The Hebrew says you know the nefesh of the stranger, the soul, the inner life. You've been the one at the edge. You've been the one without rights. Use that memory. The Talmud counts how often this comes up. One sage says the Torah warns about the stranger in thirty-six places; others say forty-six. Either way, few commands are repeated so often. This isn't even the first time in this portion; a chapter earlier, the same warning appears. It seems the Torah expected people to forget, and kept reminding them.
screen: `A STRANGER SHALT THOU NOT OPPRESS.` · `GER: ONE WHO SOJOURNS.` · `YOU KNOW THE STRANGER'S NEFESH.` · `THIRTY-SIX TIMES, OR FORTY-SIX.` · then, large: `YOU KNOW THE STRANGER'S HEART.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember being the stranger. Settle, and breathe. Bring back a time you were the new one. A school, a job, a country, a family you married into. What did it feel like in your body? Where did you not know where to stand? Who, if anyone, made room for you? Let that memory be vivid for a moment. Then think of someone new in your life now, at work, on your street, in your community. What would have helped you then? The bell holds the time.
Ger. The stranger, the one who sojourns among you. And the Torah's reason for kindness to them: you were strangers too.
Your line: you know the stranger's heart. Today, do one kind thing for a newcomer: an introduction, directions, a seat saved, a name learned. Day three hundred forty-nine.

howItsDone: Jewish communities often cite the command to love and protect the stranger when welcoming newcomers and immigrants, and the memory of being strangers in Egypt is retold every year at the Passover seder.
